title: The hours
hook: monks stop work seven times a day to pray: nothing is to be preferred to the work of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, conversatio, the Benedictine promise to keep turning. Your line was always beginning. Did your one small change hold, or did you get to start again? Day one thousand one hundred fifteen.

"Seven times a day do I praise thee." That's a line from Psalm 119, and Benedict took it at its word. In his Rule he builds the monastery's day around it: seven times in the daylight hours, the community stops and goes to chapel to pray. And then he adds another line from the same psalm, "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee," so there's prayer in the night as well. The bell rings, and whatever's in your hands goes down. The bread half kneaded. The book open at the page. The row half hoed. Christians call this rhythm the hours, or the Divine Office, and it's still kept in monasteries, and by some people outside them. Today's word: the hours.

The hours have old names. Lauds at daybreak, then Prime. Terce, Sext and None, spread through the working day. Vespers as the light goes. Compline before sleep. Each is short: psalms, a reading, a hymn, a prayer. The heart of it is the Psalms, sung or said together, and the Rule sets them out so the community prays through the whole psalter every week. Then comes the signal. In the chapter on what to do when it sounds, Benedict says: as soon as you hear it, leave whatever you have in hand and go, quickly, but with seriousness, not giddy. And then the phrase this day is built on. Nothing, he says, is to be put before the Work of God. That's his name for the hours: the Work of God, opus Dei. Not a break from work. Work. The hours don't pull the monk away from life. They stitch it together. Kitchen, field, library, chapel, kitchen again. Prayer isn't a separate compartment. It's the thread running through the day, pulling it tight at regular points so the day can't unravel into one long blur. The Bible already knew the shape. A psalm says, "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." Daniel, in Babylon, kneels three times a day and gives thanks, even when it's against the law. The monks just set the clock by it. An ordinary office worker can do a small version. Stop. Put the thing down. Turn toward God, or simply toward the quiet, for a minute. Pick it back up.

Here's the practice: stop three times today to pray. Right now, choose your three. Morning, noon and evening, or three moments that already happen: the first coffee, lunch, the drive home. Set a reminder if that helps. Then try the first one now. Put down whatever's in your hands. Sit still. If you pray, you can say a line of a psalm you know, or simply say God's name. If you don't, just stop, and notice the day you're in. The bell holds the time.
The hours. The Divine Office: set times of prayer through the day and night, which Benedict calls the Work of God.
Your line: nothing before prayer. Today, at your three times, put down what's in your hands first, even mid-sentence. Then pick it back up. Day one thousand one hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns pray the hours together in chapel at set times of day and night; some Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran Christians pray a shorter form at home, often morning and evening prayer.

notes: Rule 16 quotes Psalm 119:164 (seven times) and 119:62 (midnight) and names the day hours; the script's 'seven times in the daylight hours' plus night prayer follows Rule 16. Check the list of hour names against Rule 16 (it names Matins/Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, Compline; Prime is not named in the script).

'Prays through the whole psalter every week' follows Rule 18; confirm.
Rule 43: at the signal leave whatever is in hand and hasten, with gravity so as not to give occasion for levity; 'nothing is to be preferred to the Work of God'. Paraphrased.
